Consult Summary:
33-year-old male with 3-day history of acute watery/loose diarrhea (4–5/day) with mild abdominal pain and single episode of vomiting; no red-flag features (blood, mucus, severe dehydration). Telehealth advice given for presumed self-limiting gastroenteritis.

History:
• Onset: Diarrhea began 3 days ago.  
• Course: Persistent; neither clearly improving nor worsening.  
• Frequency: 4–5 bowel motions/day; variable consistency (watery to loose).  
• Associated symptoms: Mild abdominal pain; one episode of vomiting; subjective mild fever; reduced appetite.  
• Denies: Blood or mucus in stool, recent travel, high-risk/“dodgy” food, severe fever, severe abdominal pain.  
• Hydration: Drinking fluids well; no signs of clinical dehydration observed on video.  
• No medications taken yet for diarrhea or pain.  
• Review of systems otherwise non-contributory (no respiratory, urinary, chest pain, neurologic complaints mentioned).

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – childhood onset, still using inhaler.  
  – Control level, exacerbation history, and complications not discussed.

Medications:
• “Lexapro” inhaler (patient report; details unclear, conflict noted – Lexapro is typically oral escitalopram, not an inhaler). Dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No other regular, PRN, or over-the-counter medications reported.

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Location: Lives in London (address confirmed).  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drug use, occupation, and living situation not discussed.

Family History:
• Father: Hypertension; died of bowel cancer at age 62.  
• No other familial conditions mentioned.

Physical Examination:
(telemedicine visual inspection only)  
• General: Appears well; not clinically dehydrated per physician observation.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• No additional examination findings documented.

Investigations:
• None ordered or performed during consult.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute self-limiting diarrhea/gastroenteritis  
  • Likely viral or dietary; low risk features at present.  
  • Plan:  
    – Hydration: Encourage ample oral fluids; consider oral rehydration salts (Dioralyte OTC).  
    – Diet: “Soft diet” for 48 h after symptom improvement; avoid dairy, meat, fish, eggs initially. Use easily digested foods (toast, crackers, mashed vegetables).  
    – Probiotics: Yoghurt permitted to help restore gut flora.  
    – Medications: None prescribed; patient may use OTC analgesia (e.g., paracetamol) if abdominal pain increases (not explicitly discussed).  
    – Monitoring:  
        • Seek care if stools ≥6–8/day, signs of dehydration, high fever, severe pain.  
        • Re-contact clinician or urgent care if blood or mucus appears, or if diarrhea persists >1 week.  
        • Stool culture to be arranged if red-flag signs develop.

General Plan items:  
• Consultation summary entered into patient app for review.  
• No follow-up booked; to call back PRN per above warning signs.  
• Advised to continue asthma inhaler as usual.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: vitals, comprehensive medication reconciliation, smoking/alcohol history, detailed asthma control history.  
• Internal conflict: Patient states using “Lexapro” inhaler for asthma; Lexapro is an oral SSRI. Clarification required.  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor inaudible sections but clinical details preserved.
